measurement.happened:
This week in Turkey was dominated by three major threads: the launch of COP31, a widening financial corruption scandal, and a deadly industrial explosion, all set against a backdrop of active diplomacy and social protest.

COP31 and the energy transition. The UN climate summit kicked off in Turkey on November 9, and the country spent the entire week preparing for it. Turkey unveiled a 2040 energy plan built around electricity that requires roughly 500 billion dollars in investment, and the government's message was clear: electrify everything, push recycling, and try not to talk about coal (Reuters, AP, AFP, DW, TV5Monde, FT, Bloomberg). The country is showcasing a genuine solar and renewables surge, but coal and other fossil fuels still loom large in the mix (AP, AFP, DW). Satellite data revealed a significant landfill methane problem just before the summit (Reuters). Villagers in coal-mining regions demanded that COP31 delegates come see the devastation firsthand, with one mother and daughter leading a local fight against a mine they call a 'pit of hell' (Reuters, AFP, TV5Monde). Farmers are struggling to adapt as droughts intensify (Reuters). The Financial Times noted a 'terrible backdrop' of extreme weather over the past year (FT). Bloomberg reported that bankers are preparing for AI to feature in every conversation at the summit. The US is sending lawmakers to the talks (Reuters). There is also a zero-waste ambition that clashes with the recycling reality on the ground (FT). War-driven refugees in Turkey are finding it harder to leave as climate change worsens their situation (Bloomberg).

The fund manipulation scandal. This was the week's biggest domestic political story. Former minister Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya was arrested (Reuters, AP, DW, Bloomberg). The Borsa Istanbul CEO was detained (Bloomberg, FT). The market clearinghouse CEO resigned (Bloomberg). The Turkish stock market chief was arrested (Bloomberg). A former regulatory executive was arrested (Bloomberg). Six people in total were ordered detained (Reuters, NTV). Frozen funds' blue-chip holdings were sold off-market (Bloomberg). The Financial Times called it a 20-billion-dollar fraud and compared it to a Ponzi scheme, coining the phrase 'From Ponzi to Fonzi' (FT). Private backers stepped back from Turkey's flagship EV project Togg, possibly linked to the scandal (Bloomberg). The probe is clearly widening and touching multiple levels of the financial establishment.

Steel plant explosion. On November 9, a major explosion at a steel plant in Izmir killed at least 16 people (some early reports said 10 dead and 4 missing) (Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, TV5Monde, Bloomberg). The plant belonged to a top Turkish steel exporter (Bloomberg). Erdogan promised to find the truth (TV5Monde). This adds to a week that also saw eight people killed in a series of shootings in rural western Turkey (BBC, TV5Monde).

Defense and diplomacy. Turkey's parliament approved a three-nation defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan amid mounting Houthi attacks (Reuters, AP). Turkey and Azerbaijan denied speculation that their relationship was fraying, and Erdogan personally joined an Azerbaijani victory celebration in a visible sign of thaw (Reuters, AP, TV5Monde, Bloomberg). Turkey said a gas pipeline project with Turkish Cypriots could provide power to the whole island (Reuters). Erdogan said he wants to discuss ending the Russia-Ukraine war with Putin after talks with Zelenskiy (Reuters). The US slapped sanctions on Indian and Turkish firms and people for aiding Iran (Reuters). South Korea and Turkey agreed to cooperate in nuclear, defense, and infrastructure (Reuters). Turkey's 34-billion-dollar military pension fund entered the Libyan oil trade (Bloomberg). The Financial Times and TV5Monde both asked whether Turkey is becoming a new regional power (FT, TV5Monde). Turkey also pushed back against EU comments on its rights record and judiciary, calling them 'prejudiced and unfair' (Reuters).

Media protests and social tension. Thousands of people took to the streets in multiple cities to protest a crackdown on media, the arrest of journalists, and media shutdowns (AFP, two separate headlines). This suggests a growing public frustration with press freedom.

Miscellaneous. Fenerbahce beat Liverpool 3-2 in Istanbul in a Champions League match, exposing weaknesses in the Reds (BBC). The Kurdish club Amedspor is shaking up Turkish football (Al Jazeera). Jailed PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan was moved to a new section of his island prison (Al Jazeera). Turkey's inflation quickened unexpectedly, clouding the central bank's rate path (Bloomberg). There was a lighthearted CNN piece about 1,000-year-old Viking graffiti in an Istanbul landmark and a travel piece about the 'Turkish Maldives' (CNN).
measurement.expected:
COP31 negotiations (almost certain). The summit is now underway in Turkey, so the coming week will be filled with bilateral and multilateral climate negotiations, side events, and political speeches. Turkey will push its electrification and renewables narrative while trying to keep coal off the formal agenda. Expect at least one or two notable bilateral deals or announcements involving Turkey, possibly around the gas pipeline with Cyprus or the 500-billion-dollar energy investment plan. The 'don't mention coal' strategy will be tested as delegates press for specifics. There will likely be at least one protest or demonstration outside the venue, given the coal-mine communities already mobilizing. Confidence: almost certain.

Fund scandal developments (probable). The arrests of the former minister, the stock exchange CEO, the clearinghouse CEO, and the regulatory executive suggest the probe is in its active phase. In the coming week, expect at least one or two more detentions or arrests as investigators follow money trails. The Borsa Istanbul may see increased volatility as frozen funds continue to be unwound. The Togg EV project may face further uncertainty as private backers reconsider their positions. There is a real chance the government faces a parliamentary question or a minor political spat over how the probe is being handled, given that a former Erdogan-era minister is involved. Confidence: probable for further arrests and market jitters; possible for a parliamentary flashpoint.

Steel plant aftermath (probable). The Izmir explosion will dominate domestic news for several days. Expect the government to announce a formal investigation, possibly a temporary halt to operations at the plant or similar facilities, and a public statement from Erdogan or the relevant minister. There may be a small workers' demonstration or a moment of national mourning. The opposition will use it to press questions about industrial safety standards. Confidence: probable.

Turkey-Azerbaijan and defense diplomacy (possible). The visible thaw with Azerbaijan and the newly ratified Saudi-Pakistan defense pact suggest Turkey is actively expanding its security partnerships. In the coming week, expect follow-up statements, possibly a joint military exercise announcement or a further diplomatic meeting. The Erdogan-Putin-Zelenskiy triangle may see a phone call or a brief statement, but a full trilateral meeting is unlikely in just one week. The US sanctions on Turkish firms for aiding Iran will likely prompt a Turkish foreign ministry response and possibly a retaliatory measure or at least a pointed statement. Confidence: possible for further diplomatic moves; unlikely for a major new agreement to be signed this week.

Media protests (possible). The thousands who protested journalists' arrests and media shutdowns suggest the issue is not yet resolved. If no prominent journalist is released or no media outlet is restored in the coming days, a second wave of protest is possible, perhaps smaller in scale. The government may either make a small concession (releasing one or two journalists) or double down, in which case the protests could grow. Confidence: possible for a follow-up demonstration.

Inflation and monetary policy (possible). The unexpected uptick in inflation noted by Bloomberg will keep the central bank under pressure. A rate decision or at least a signal from the central bank is possible within the next week, though a full policy meeting may fall just outside this window. The lira may see some volatility. Confidence: possible for a central bank statement or market reaction.

Less likely surprises: a second industrial accident or a small earthquake in the Izmir or Aegean region (possible but not expected); a sudden announcement that Ocalan will be granted a minor concession in his prison conditions (unlikely); a surprise visit by a foreign head of state to Ankara during the COP31 window (possible but not in the cards); a minor data leak or cyber incident tied to the fund probe (unlikely). Things I would not bet on: a full cabinet reshuffle this week; a major military operation or border incident with Greece or Syria; a change in the central bank governor; a new constitutional referendum; or Turkey formally leaving or joining a major trade bloc. None of these have enough momentum in the headlines to materialize in a single week.
emoji_reasons: COP31 kicked off in Turkey and the entire week was framed around the country's energy transition, climate promises, and the tension between its renewables boom and its continued reliance on coal.

The $20 billion fund manipulation scandal produced a cascade of arrests including a former minister, the stock exchange CEO, and the clearinghouse chief, making it the week's defining domestic political drama.
The Izmir steel plant explosion that killed at least 16 workers was the single most dramatic event of the week and will shape domestic politics and industrial-safety debate for days to come.

delta.motion:
The financial crisis grew from a contained brokerage-and-fund probe into a full-blown corruption scandal touching ministers, regulators, and even the flagship EV project. In the first photograph the story was about a detained CEO, a cancelled licence, and a panicked fivefold raise in the investor bar. By the second photograph, a former minister has been arrested, the clearinghouse CEO has resigned, the stock-market chief is in custody, a former regulatory executive is detained, six people in total are under arrest, frozen blue-chip holdings have been sold off-market, and the Financial Times is calling it a twenty-billion-dollar Ponzi scheme. The Togg EV project losing private backers is a new thread that ties the scandal to industrial policy. The speed of the widening is notable: within eight days the probe moved from the brokerage floor to the ministerial cabinet and to the government's most visible industrial showcase.

COP31 grew from an upcoming event mentioned in passing to the single largest international story of the week. The first photograph noted it as a platform Erdogan would use to reinforce Turkey's mediator brand. The second photograph shows the summit fully launched with a 2040 energy plan, a five-hundred-billion-dollar investment figure, a public fight over coal versus renewables, satellite data exposing landfill methane, villagers in mining regions demanding delegates visit their sites, farmers struggling with drought, and a zero-waste ambition that clashes with recycling reality. The theme expanded from a diplomatic occasion to a full domestic-policy stress test.

The media-protest theme persisted and arguably intensified. The first photograph recorded the October 24 street demonstrations and the opposition's public denunciation. The second photograph reports thousands again in the streets across multiple cities, citing arrests of journalists and shutdowns of outlets. The rhythm is now weekly rather than episodic, which suggests the government has not resolved the underlying tension.

The Azerbaijan rift shrank and nearly resolved. In the first photograph Aliyev had skipped a Turkey-hosted summit and arrests were ordered over a headscarf criticism. In the second photograph both governments denied the relationship was fraying, and Erdogan personally joined an Azerbaijani victory celebration in a visible thaw. The snub that dominated the first week is now a footnote.

The Zelenskiy visit shrank from an active diplomatic event to a talking point. The first photograph captured his arrival and the mediation angle. The second photograph reduces it to Erdogan saying he wants to discuss ending the war with Putin after the talks. The visit is done; the follow-up is a sentence in a statement.

The Turkey-Libya maritime dispute with Greece, which in the first photograph was a sharp escalation with the Greek PM calling the deal void and three Arab states lining up behind Athens, largely vanished from the second photograph's headlines. The Cyprus gas pipeline is a new maritime item but a different story. The Greece-Libya fight did not sustain its momentum into the second week.

The UN Secretary-General race, the Cappadocia rock collapse, the Volkswagen-Dogus car letter, the CalMac ferry delay, the Mohamed Salah transfer, the Marti Technologies expansion, and the tornado all appeared in the first photograph and are absent from the second. They were single-week stories that the news cycle moved past.

New items that appeared only in the second photograph include the Izmir steel-plant explosion that killed at least sixteen people, eight people killed in rural western Turkey shootings, Turkey's inflation quickening unexpectedly, US sanctions on Turkish and Indian firms for aiding Iran, a South Korea-Turkey cooperation deal on nuclear and defense, the military pension fund entering the Libyan oil trade, Fenerbahce beating Liverpool in the Champions League, Amedspor disrupting Turkish football, Turkey pushing back against EU comments on its judiciary, and the Togg EV link to the fund scandal. The steel explosion and the rural shootings are the most consequential new arrivals, adding a layer of domestic fragility that was not present in the first week.
delta.wind:
The financial-crisis forecast was the closest to reality. The expectation was almost certain that the crisis would dominate and probable that new names would be arrested or step down. That is exactly what happened, and the scope exceeded the forecast: a former minister was arrested, not just a CEO; the FT framed it as a twenty-billion-dollar Ponzi; and the Togg connection was not anticipated. The 'almost certain' confidence was well calibrated.

The Zelenskiy follow-up expectation was also met. The forecast said almost certain for a joint statement or summary and probable for modest diplomatic output. Erdogan's statement about wanting to discuss ending the war with Putin after the talks is precisely the kind of modest output predicted. This came true at the expected level.

COP31 was forecast as almost certain to be a major story and probable to intersect with media and protest themes. Both parts came true. The summit dominated the international coverage, and the intersection with domestic social issues (villagers protesting the mine, farmers in drought, the methane data) gave environmental and opposition voices a platform. The forecast got this right.

The media-protest expectation was probable that the theme persists and possible that a new incident triggers a second wave. The second photograph confirms thousands back in the streets in multiple cities. The theme persisted, and the second wave materialized. The forecast was accurate, though one could argue the 'possible' was slightly too cautious given that the protests had already become a weekly rhythm.

The Black Sea and Greece-Libya forecast was probable for continued rhetorical friction and possible for a new Turkish statement or small naval exercise. This is where the expectation was most off. The dispute largely faded from the headlines in the second week. No naval exercise, no major new Turkish statement on the Libya deal. The friction did not sustain. The forecast overestimated the momentum of the Greece-Libya fight, perhaps because the first week's headlines (Greek PM calling the deal void, three Arab states backing Greece) made it feel like an escalation that would continue, but in practice the diplomatic sparring lost its news value once the initial shock wore off.

The Azerbaijan forecast was possible for further commentary and unlikely for a major new development. Reality was more positive than the forecast allowed: the rift visibly thawed, with both sides denying the fraying and Erdogan joining a celebration. The 'possible for commentary' was true but understated; the actual outcome was a small repair, which the forecast had placed in the 'less likely surprises' bucket. The expectation was too conservative here.

The Iran and defense-pact forecast was probable for a formal step on the defense pact and possible for another round of Iran diplomacy. The parliament formally approved the three-nation pact, which is exactly the formal step predicted. The US sanctions on Turkish firms for aiding Iran is a new Iran-adjacent development that was not specifically forecast but fits the 'possible for another round' category. This came true.

The Kurdish peace forecast was possible for a small follow-up and unlikely for a major shift. Ocalan's move to a new section of the prison is reported again, but it is the same gesture, not a new one. No major shift. The forecast was accurate at the expected level.

The Cappadocia forecast was probable for an investigation announcement and a safety review, possible for a tourism dip. The story simply vanished from the second photograph's headlines. The investigation presumably happened but did not generate new front-page coverage. The forecast was directionally right (the story would fade) but the 'probable for an investigation announcement' as a headline event did not materialize in the second week's news cycle.

The UN chief race forecast was possible for some diplomatic movement and unlikely for a decisive step. The story vanished entirely. The 'possible' was too generous; in practice it was closer to 'unlikely.' The name was thrown in, got a day of coverage, and the news cycle moved on.

Things that were not expected and appeared: the Izmir steel-plant explosion killing sixteen, the rural western Turkey shootings killing eight, the unexpected inflation acceleration, the US sanctions on Turkish firms, the South Korea cooperation deal, the Togg EV connection to the scandal, the military pension fund in Libyan oil, and the Fenerbahce-Liverpool match. The steel explosion is the biggest miss. The 'less likely surprises' list included a sudden resignation of a senior minister, a new round of media arrests, a naval confrontation, a Turkish-Azerbaijan joint statement, a major earthquake, and a sudden Ocalan shift. None of those exact items appeared, but the steel explosion and the rural shootings are in the same family of high-impact domestic events that the forecast acknowledged as low-probability, high-impact risks. The forecast's instinct to list 'a major earthquake or natural disaster' as a low-probability risk was the right category, but a steel-plant explosion is not a natural disaster and was not explicitly listed.

The overall pattern of error: the forecast overestimated the persistence of multi-actor diplomatic disputes (Greece-Libya, UN race) and underestimated the speed at which a domestic political rift could repair itself (Azerbaijan). It also underestimated the speed and depth of the financial scandal's widening, and it did not anticipate a major industrial accident. The forecast was strongest on the themes that were already in motion (financial crisis, COP31, media protests, defense pact) and weakest on the themes that depended on multiple foreign actors sustaining momentum (Greece-Libya, UN race).
delta.driver: The force moving Turkey from the first photograph to the second is the collision between a deepening domestic corruption scandal and a government that is simultaneously trying to lock in its position as a regional power on a global stage. The fund-and-brokerage probe that began as a technical market failure has become a political trial of the Erdogan government's economic credibility, and the arrests of a former minister and multiple regulators show that the probe is no longer contained to the financial sector but is touching the cabinet and the state's most visible industrial project. At the same time, COP31 has handed Turkey a two-week global audience in which to project competence, openness, and a credible energy-transition story, which forces the government to manage the scandal's optics in real time while world leaders are watching. The formal approval of the Saudi-Pakistan defense pact, the visible thaw with Azerbaijan, the Zelenskiy-Putin mediation thread, and the South Korea deal all feed the same narrative: Turkey is consolidating a security and economic architecture that positions Ankara as a bridge power. The street, however, is asserting a counternarrative through the media protests and the shock of the Izmir steel explosion, reminding the government that domestic fragility is not a thing that can be managed away with diplomatic summits. The underlying tension is between a government that wants to be seen as a confident regional architect and a domestic public that is watching ministers and regulators go into custody, inflation tick up, and a steel plant kill sixteen workers, and the eight-day gap between the two photographs is the space in which that tension played out in real time.

The summit will not produce a single dramatic breakthrough or collapse; it will produce a negotiating text, side events, and a steady drumbeat of bilateral meetings. Confidence: high.

Fund scandal and political consequences: Almost certain the scandal remains the top domestic story. Probable for a new specific development beyond the six current arrests: a parliamentary question or committee hearing, a ministerial reshuffle or another resignation, a Togg-related announcement (government stepping in, a new backer, or a formal restructuring), or a secondary market reaction to the off-market sale of frozen blue-chip holdings. The FT's 'Ponzi to Fonzi' framing will be picked up by more outlets. The connection to the Togg EV project is the most likely new thread to develop, because it ties the scandal to the government's most visible industrial showcase and gives the opposition a concrete policy failure to attack. The central bank's rate path remains clouded by the inflation acceleration, and a short central-bank statement or a bond-market wobble is possible but not certain. I would not bet on a full banking crisis or a lira drop of more than two percent in the week. Confidence: high for continued prominence, moderate for a specific new development.

Media protests and the street: Almost certain the theme persists into next week, given the weekly rhythm established over the past two weeks. Probable for a new trigger: another journalist arrest, a new outlet shutdown, or a court ruling on a media case. The protests will likely be visible in Istanbul and at least one other city. The intersection with COP31 is significant: foreign delegates and camera crews will see the protests, and the government will be managing two narratives simultaneously (openness and competence at the summit, control at home). The opposition in parliament will use the scandal and the protests together in at least one public statement. I would not bet on a government concession that fully resolves the tension, but a small symbolic gesture (a statement, a meeting with journalists, a temporary pause in enforcement) is possible. Confidence: high for persistence, moderate for a new trigger.

Izmir steel explosion and industrial safety: Probable for investigation news, a safety review across the steel and manufacturing sector, and political blame. The opposition will use the accident to attack the government's industrial policy, and the government will promise an inquiry. The company's stock will likely be volatile. The rural western Turkey shootings (eight dead) will generate a day or two of coverage but are unlikely to sustain a full week. I would not bet on a second major industrial accident in the same week, though the narrative priming makes one more newsworthy. Confidence: moderate for investigation and safety news, low for a second accident.

Diplomatic and defense follow-ups: Probable for one modest diplomatic event: most likely a Turkish response to the US sanctions on firms aiding Iran (a foreign-ministry statement, a quiet negotiation, or a small counter-measure), or an Erdogan-Putin phone call or meeting announcement following the Zelenskiy talks. The South Korea cooperation deal, the Cyprus gas pipeline, and the military pension fund in Libyan oil will each produce a sentence or two but are unlikely to sustain headline coverage, consistent with the wind's warning about multi-actor threads fading. The Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact, now approved, will enter an implementation phase that is quieter than the ratification drama. The Azerbaijan thaw will hold; I would not bet on a new rift. The EU-judiciary pushback will generate a foreign-ministry statement but not a new crisis. Confidence: moderate for one diplomatic follow-up, low for a new crisis.

Inflation and economic background: Possible for a central-bank statement or a bond-market reaction, but the inflation acceleration is more likely to be a background variable that feeds the fund-scandal narrative than a standalone headline. The lira may wobble modestly. I would not bet on an emergency rate cut or a major economic announcement in the week. Confidence: low-moderate for a standalone economic headline.

Less likely surprises the motion makes more probable: A Togg development (government takeover, a dramatic backer exit, or a formal restructuring) is more likely than it looks because the scandal has already touched the project and the government cannot let its flagship EV story die quietly. A second industrial accident or workplace disaster is more likely than a random week would suggest because the steel explosion has primed the narrative and safety inspections are now active. A parliamentary motion of no confidence or a ministerial reshuffle is more likely than it looks because the fund scandal has now touched a former minister and the opposition has a concrete policy failure (Togg) to pair with the media protests. A COP31 side-deal or a unilateral Erdogan announcement (a new energy fund, a regional climate pact) is more likely than it looks because the summit gives him a global audience and a two-week window to lock in a legacy moment.

What I would not bet on: A full banking crisis or a lira crash above two percent. A military confrontation with Greece, Libya, or another neighbor. A sudden Ocalan release or a major shift in the Kurdish peace process. The South Korea deal, the Cyprus gas pipeline, or the military pension fund generating sustained multi-day coverage. A new major natural disaster (earthquake, flood, tornado) in the same week, though possible. A full government concession on media freedom that ends the protest cycle. A reversal of the 2040 energy plan or a dramatic COP31 collapse.
crystal.headline: COP31 Spotlight Sharpens as Fund Scandal Swallows Another Layer of Turkish Power
emoji_reasons: The fund-and-brokerage scandal is the dominant domestic drama, with arrests, resignations, and a possible Togg reckangement making it the week's central political theater.
COP31 is the defining international event of the week, putting Turkey's energy plan and climate credibility on a global stage for a full week of negotiations.
Media protests have become a weekly rhythm and will almost certainly continue, with the added pressure of foreign delegates watching Turkey manage its press-freedom image during the summit.
crystal.tldr: COP31 will dominate Turkey's international coverage while the fund-and-brokerage scandal accelerates into a political reckangement, likely producing a parliamentary hearing, a Togg development, or another high-profile arrest. Media protests will continue their weekly cadence, and the Izmir steel explosion will generate investigation and safety-review news, but no single diplomatic thread from the past two weeks is likely to sustain a full week of headlines.
crystal.eli5:
Turkey is hosting a huge climate meeting called COP31 right now, and it will be the biggest story in the world for the next week. The government wants to show everyone that Turkey is serious about clean energy, but there are real problems: too much coal, farmers struggling with drought, and a methane leak from a big landfill that satellite pictures just revealed. Expect a lot of talking, some arguments, and the Turkish president trying to look like a world leader.

At the same time, there is a big money scandal at home. A lot of people who run the stock market and a former government minister have been arrested because they allegedly moved billions of dollars around in a way that looks like a giant scam. The government's own electric-car project might be losing its investors because of this. Next week, more people could get arrested, a committee in parliament might hold a hearing, and the car project could get a major update. It is getting more serious every day.

And then there are the protests. For two weeks in a row, thousands of people have marched in the streets because the government has been cracking down on TV channels and newspapers. This is probably going to happen again next week, and it will be awkward because all the foreign climate delegates will be walking around Istanbul and seeing it.

There was also a big explosion at a steel factory in Izmir that killed sixteen workers, and eight more people were shot dead in a small town in the west. These are sad and serious, and the government will promise to investigate, but they are less likely to keep the headlines for a full week compared to the money scandal and the climate meeting.

The one thing I would not bet on is a big fight with a neighbor country or a sudden change in the president's plans. The small diplomatic deals Turkey has been making with South Korea, Cyprus, and others will probably get a sentence in the news and then fade, just like last week's argument with Greece and Libya did.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A saw the week's major themes correctly and with appropriate confidence. Its call that the fund crisis would remain the dominant domestic story was spot-on: six people were ordered detained, the Borsa Istanbul CEO was jailed, the clearinghouse CEO resigned, a former minister was arrested, and the FT branded it a $20 billion Ponzi-like fraud. A's prediction of 'at least one or two more arrests or resignations' was actually conservative — there were multiple. A correctly flagged COP31 as an 'almost certain' major story, and the summit indeed generated extensive coverage of Turkey's 2040 energy plan, the coal question, farmer and villager protests, and the methane problem. A's Zelenskiy follow-up prediction was accurate: Erdogan publicly said he wants to discuss ending the war with Putin after the Istanbul talks, reinforcing Turkey's mediator brand. A's media-protest call was right — thousands marched in multiple cities over journalist arrests and outlet shutdowns. A's defense-pact prediction ('probable for a formal step') matched the parliamentary approval of the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey pact. A's Azerbaijan section ('possible for further commentary; unlikely for a major new development') was broadly correct in that the rift stayed in the news, though it slightly understated the positive thaw — Erdogan personally joined an Azerbaijani victory celebration, a visible gesture of unity. A's Kurdish-process call (small step, no breakthrough) matched Ocalan's move to a new prison section. A's Greece-Libya section was reasonable: the dispute continued (EU comments, Libyan oil trade by the military pension fund) without a naval clash. A's 'less likely surprises' list was well-calibrated — none of those surprises materialized. What A missed: the steel plant explosion in Izmir that killed at least 16 people (a major event with Erdogan's 'we will find the truth' promise), the eight killed in rural western-Turkey shootings, the Togg EV project losing private backers (a direct spillover of the fund crisis that A did not explicitly connect), the South Korea-Turkey nuclear/defense/infrastructure cooperation, the gas-pipeline project with Turkish Cypriots, and the broader 'new regional power' framing that FT and TV5Monde pushed. A also gave Cappadocia and the UN Secretary-General race their own sections, but neither was a major story this week, so those were minor overweights. Overall, A's picture of the week was substantially correct on the dominant threads and well-calibrated on probabilities.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B also captured the week's major threads with reasonable accuracy. Its fund-crisis section correctly identified the story as dominant and predicted additional arrests and regulatory moves, all of which happened (six detained, multiple arrests, clearinghouse CEO resignation).
